question: to the Commission Céline Imart (PPE), Gilles Pennelle (PfE), Cristina Maestre (S&D), Daniele Polato (ECR), Sarah Knafo (ESN), Volker Schnurrbusch (ESN), Isabelle Le Callennec (PPE), Christophe Gomart (PPE), Valérie Deloge (PfE) Subject:

Following an application submitted by Guinea, in January 2026 the Commission published a Traditional Speciality Guaranteed (TSG) registration for ‘Fleur de Sel’. This TSG appears highly problematic, as it is based on a specification that is not shared by all existing or pending Protected Geographical Indications (PGIs), such as ‘Fleur de Sel de Camargue’, nor by the national rules of several Member States regulating flower of salt. These products are clearly identified by consumers, fully comply with the chemical and organoleptic characteristics that distinguish fleur de sel from coarse salt, and are rooted in local practices determined by their specific environments. Furthermore, the creation of an overarching TSG would weaken the legal protection afforded to PGIs for fleur de sel by encouraging the use of generic designations that run counter to the very purpose of the PGI system and would conflict with national rules of several Member States. In this context: 1.
How does the Commission intend to safeguard the integrity of existing PGIs and those currently undergoing the registration process?

Should the Commission not reclassify the TSG application as an application for the PGI ‘Guinean Fleur de Sel’, thereby ensuring recognition of the specific characteristics of its own production method?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (26.8.2026) The registration and protection of geographical indications (GIs) and traditional specialities guaranteed (TSG) are governed by Regulation (EU) 2024/11431, which lays down distinct conditions and procedures for each scheme. The Commission applies those rules in a manner that preserves the integrity of each scheme and the protection of registered names. It examines each application carefully, including possible conflicts with earlier rights and compliance with the relevant rules. TSG applications are examined taking into account the protection of registered Protected Geographical Indications (PGIs) and Protected Designations of Origin (PDOs), as well as any pending PGI or PDO applications, in accordance with the applicable legal requirements. The application to register ‘Fleur de sel/Flor de sal/Solni cvet’ as a TSG was published in the registration but opened the opposition procedure, allowing interested parties to submit an opposition under the applicable rules. The Commission is examining the application under the relevant legal framework. The Commission cannot unilaterally reclassify a TSG application as a PGI application. The two schemes are legally distinct and subject to different requirements and procedures. It is for the applicant to decide under which scheme an application is submitted. Any application to register a name such as ‘Guinean Fleur de Sel’ as a PGI would need to be submitted separately and would have to demonstrate compliance with Regulation (EU) 2024/1143, including the required link between a given quality, reputation or other characteristic of the product and the defined geographical area.
1 Regulation (EU) 2024/1143 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 11 April 2024 on geographical
indications for wine, spirit drinks and agricultural products, as well as traditional specialities guaranteed and optional quality terms for agricultural products.
